text.p: These are the main stories in Latvian newspapers on Monday. Prepared for Reuters by the Cooperation Fund. Reuters has not verified these reports and does not vouch for their accuracy:
- A business centre at Ventspils commercial port was opened on Saturday.
- A ship with 50 Latvian passengers on board was taken into charge by Swedish authorities for tax arrears. Its passengers and crew were sent back to Latvia by plane.

- Prime Minister Andris Shkele believes the government party council should decide whether ministers who are not in a political party may work in the government. The case has arisen after Finance Minister Aivars Kreituss was expelled from the Saimnieks Party, the largest group in the coalition.

- Russian Minister of Transport Valery Zaitsev said Russia is not going to reintroduce tax reductions for cargos transported via Latvian ports, abolished from September 1, because cargo turnover in this direction is expected to grow by 17 percent per month. His Latvian counterpart Vilis Kristopans forecasts cargos being transported to Latvian ports will fall 10 to 15 percent a month.
- According to experts of the Council of Europe and the Latvian ministry of welfare Latvia's legislation makes it ready to sign Europe's Social Charter.
- The sixth international cinema forum Arsenals opens today in Riga. A total of 225 films will be shown.
- The Latvian company of the Baltic peace-keeping battalion has gone to Sweden to be trained in carrying out peace-keeping operations. In October, 50 of them will go to Bosnia.

- There was a confidential telephone conversation between the prime ministers of Latvia and Lithuania last Thursday, with the contents hidden from the heads of the delegations negotiating their border settlement. The Latvian prime minister's foreign policy advisor Aivars Groza said Shkele would possibly not insist on ratification of the licence agreement with Amoco and Swedish Olje Prospektering before receiving an official reply from Lithuania.
- Insurance company Balta has doubled its stock capital and is now the largest insurer in the Baltics.
